topics.text:

topics.title: Venn Diagram Tourney
topics.text:
I have decided to host a Venn diagram tourney, as a second tourney to the Trapezoid Tourney. It is also the fourth and final contest I will have this year.



The tourney is only available for this year, as it is a one time tourney and no other years will I do this tourney again, as I will be working on a different tourney, which I will post about in the Contests & Programs forum later.



There are two parts to the tourney, and the rules are quite simple, even though one part is on FTW. For the FTW tourney, it will be a very simple game. People will play each other in pairs, with the scoring method responses and 44 seconds per problem. This is to give you one second less, as many times I have solved it in 44.5 seconds without guessing. :) Then, the winners of a round will move on to the written portion, which I already have the problems for.



The written portion will be a 20 question 8 minute test, about Venn diagrams and complex things about it. This is not a regular test they give at school about Venn diagrams. The test is easy for the beginning problems, about the school round/early chapter sprint mathcounts level, with the further problems the middle/late chapter round. 8 minutes should be enough, as long as you know your Venn diagrams. IF its not, then those who didn't submit on time, I won't count it against you. You will need to draw certain things, so be prepared to use asymptote or draw on paper then attach it to your submission. You may be able to google some theorems that you don't know, but please do not do so until after the test (before the test is okay, as you are preparing for it. Just not during the test.)



The FTW part will be on 8/22/17, 6PM ET

The written part will be as soon as I get the results from FTW. I will PM you a link to a private forum about the test, where answers are submitted through a new PM. The time limit is by honor system, but answers are due by September 3.

Top Scorers will be announced within the following few days.

If you didn't make the second round but you still want to look at the test, you are allowed to. If you did well, I will post your score as well, but as an unofficial one.

IF you are banned from FTW, I will sort out a different method for you,

The questions are quite creative about Venn diagrams, so be prepared of anything that may be related to Venn diagrams.



You can sign up here or through PMs. Have fun!



EDIT: Because practically nobody showed uo for FTW, everyone will make part 2. Problems will be in a Trapezoid Tourney forum, as I reuse forums, sometime next week.

topics.title: k Is the answer key wrong.
topics.text:
I was doing the 1994 AJHSME  problems, but when I came across the 22nd question, I realized that there was a mistake in the solution.



The two wheels shown below are spun and the two resulting numbers are added. The probability that the sum is even is



IMAGE

$\text{(A)}\ \dfrac{1}{6} \qquad \text{(B)}\ \dfrac{1}{4} \qquad \text{(C)}\ \dfrac{1}{3} \qquad \text{(D)}\ \dfrac{5}{12} \qquad \text{(E)}\ \dfrac{4}{9}$



Solution[edit]

An even sum occurs when an even is added to an even or an odd is added to an odd. Looking at the areas of the regions, the chance of getting an even in the first wheel is $\frac14$ and the chance of getting an odd is $\frac34$. On the second wheel, the chance of getting an even is $\frac23$ and an odd is $\frac13$. The answer key says E, but D is correct, so take note.



\[\frac14 \cdot \frac23 + \frac34 \cdot \frac13 = \frac16 + \frac14 = \boxed{\text{(D)}\ \frac{5}{12}}\]

I thought the answer was $E, \frac{4}{9},$, but maybe I'm mistaken.

topics.title: Problem 7.60, Geometry Textbook
topics.text:
I don't see how the ladder's midpoint could ever possibly make a quarter-circle. Either, the ladder would have to turn in a way contrary to that in the problem, or it would have to extend during mid-fall, which is impossible.



At any given time, the ladder's tallest point is at a height of 1-x, while its longest distance from the wall is x. (This is given that the length of the ladder is 1.)



If, the ladder's midpoint does indeed, trace a quarter-circle, then it would meet the wall and the floor at a distance of 1/2 from the origin. The midpoint, then, would have to reach a height of $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}$, and an identical length. The tallest point of the ladder then, would be $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$, and then farthest point away from the wall would also be this value. However, these two values do not add up to 1, so this case clearly can not be possible.



Help?

topics.title: I created this problem
topics.text:
Sean writes the infinite geometric sequence:



$\frac{1}{8}+\frac{2}{8}+\frac{3}{8}+\frac{4}{8}.......$



And Tom writes the finite arithmetic series



$i^{-100}+i^{-99}+i^{-98}...............+i^{100}$.



What is the sum of Sean's infinite geometric sequence and Tom's finite arithmetic series?



solution think about it!We are told that Sean wrote an infinite geometric sequence. This makes us think about the formula:



$\frac{a}{1-r}$



Where $a$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio. We see that the first term is $1/8$ and the common ratio is also $1/8$. Plugging in these values into the formula, we get:



$\frac{\frac{1}{8}}{1-\frac{1}{8}}=\frac{\frac{1}{8}}{\frac{7}{8}} = \frac{1}{7}$



Now we can look at TOm's finite arithmetic series.



We see that adding the first and last term gives us $0$ and all of them add up to $0$ and we are only left with $i^{0}$. Using our knowledge of the laws of exponents, we find the $i^{0}=1$



Thus, our answer is $1+\frac{1}{7}=\boxed{\frac{8}{7}}$




Am I right?

Four points are chosen at random from the grid at right. What is the probability that the four points are the vertices of a rectangle whose sides are parallel to the sides of the grid?



See https://artofproblemsolving.com/ebooks/intermediate-counting-ebook/preview Problem 4.4 for diagram



The solution states that [quote]

We could constructively count the probability directly, without counting the number of rectangles. For this, we think about selecting the vertices in order, one at a time. The first vertex is arbitrarily chosen. For the second vertex, there are two exclusive possibilities:



Case 1: The second vertex is in the same row or column as the first vertex. This occurs with probability $\frac{8}{24} = \frac{1}{3}$. Then, in order to produce a valid rectangle, the third vertex must be on one of the lines containing one of the first two vertices and perpendicular to the line containing the first two vertices. There are 8 such points on these lines, and 23 points remaining to choose from, so the probability of choosing one is $\frac{8}{23}$. Finally, only one point of the 22 remaining will complete the rectangle, and the probability of choosing it is $\frac{1}{22}$.



Case 2: The second vertex is not in the same row or column as the first vertex. This occurs with probability $\frac{16}{24} = \frac23$. These two points must be opposite corners of our rectangle, so the final two points that we choose must be the other two corners. They are chosen with probability $\frac{2}{23} \cdot \frac{1}{22}$.



Therefore, the probability of choosing the four corners of a valid rectangle is: $$ \frac13 \cdot \frac {8}{23} \cdot \frac{1}{22} + \frac23 \cdot \frac{2}{23} \cdot \frac{1}{22} = \frac{12}{3 \cdot 23 \cdot 22} = \frac{2}{253}. $$[/quote]



I'm a little confused in that this solution seems to imply that the order of the vertices matters. However, the problem statement says that 4 points are chosen randomly. In addition, here is the first solution of this problem:



[quote]There are $\binom{25}{4}$ ways in which we can choose 4 vertices (without regard to order). We need to determine how many of these sets of 4 vertices produce a valid rectangle. How can we construct such a rectangle? There are a couple of different ways we could proceed.



A rectangle whose sides are parallel to the sides of the grid can be determined by choosing two rows to form the horizontal sides and choosing two columns to form the vertical sides. We can choose two rows in $\binom52 = 10$ ways and choose two columns in $\binom52 = 10$ ways, so the number of rectangles is $(10)(10) = 100$.



Therefore, 100 of the $\binom{25}{4}$ sets of 4 vertices form valid rectangles, and hence our probability is $\frac{100}{\binom{25}{4}} = \frac{2}{253}$.[/quote]



This solution implies that the order of the choice of the vertices does not matter. So can someone explain what is occurring here?

topics.title: k Back To School Math Competition
topics.text:
Because school is starting up again soon (mine has already started but I go to a weird school), I decided to create a competition series. The series will have three rounds:



Round 1) A pretty simple round consisting of question you might find in a Algebra 1, Geometry, or Algebra 2 textbook. It will be 30 questions (not multiple choice) each worth 5 points, and then 2 proofs at the end worth 10 points. Of course it will be harder than the stuff you do in school, but it will be more of a careless mistake trap then a difficult test.



Round 2) A harder test consisting of late AMC8 and Mathcounts School/Chapter type questions. It will be kind of like the Mathcounts format. A test with 30 questions, each worth one point, and then 8 harder questions at the end, each worth 2 points.



Round 3) The hardest test of them all. It will consist of questions that are the same level as AMC 10/12 or Mathcounts States. I will be formatted like the AMC 10/12, 25 questions, 6 points for a correct answer, 1.5 for leaving it blank, and 0 for getting it wrong.





There will not be a time limit for any of the test because we can't enforce that, but calculators will not be allowed. Please don't use a calculator because that will be unfair to everyone else. Also please do not talk about any of the test questions until we release the results for that round. You will probably be given a week to submit your results for each round, and there will probably be a month to a month and a half between rounds.



I have not prepared the tests yet so it will probably be a month or so before round 1 is out. You can still sign up right now if you want to though.
